title: UROFACIAL SYNDROME 1
alt_titles: FACIAL PALSY, PARTIAL, WITH URINARY ABNORMALITIES
INVERTED SMILE AND OCCULT NEUROPATHIC BLADDER

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene (613469) on chromosome 10q24.2.

checks.claim: Urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.
checks.explanation: Paper reports homozygous HPSE2 mutations as causative of UFS.

checks.claim: The HPSE2 gene is located on chromosome 10q24.2.
checks.evidence_quote: Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping.
checks.explanation: The paper places the gene at 10q24. The draft's more precise band, 10q24.2, is standard gene-location nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by congenital obstructive uropathy and abnormal facial expression. Patients present with enuresis, urinary tract infection, hydronephrosis, and voiding dysfunction as a result of neurogenic bladder (Wang et al., 1997). Daly et al. (2010) characterized the disorder by facial grimacing when attempting to smile and failure of the urinary bladder to void completely despite a lack of anatomic bladder outflow obstruction or overt neurologic damage; affected individuals often have reflux of infected urine from the bladder to the upper renal tract, with a risk of kidney damage and renal failure.

checks.claim: Urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Urofacial syndrome (UFS) is a rare autosomal recessive disease

checks.evidence_quote: failure of the urinary bladder to void completely despite a lack of anatomical bladder outflow obstruction or overt neurological damage

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families, 1 of them consanguineous (first cousins), who had peculiar facies and gestures while smiling and crying. Urinary findings included hydronephrosis, hydroureter, intravesical stenosis of the ureter, abnormal caliber of the urethra in the prostatic and membranous portions, urethral valves, and an abnormal bladder with trabeculation and diverticula associated with severe hypertrophy of the mucosa with sclerotic changes. Elejalde (1979) considered that the syndrome represented alteration of the facial and urinary developmental fields.

paragraphs.text: Between 1965 and 1986, Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) saw 36 children with enuresis and urinary tract infection in association with 'inversion' of facial expression when laughing. Urologic workup disclosed characteristic findings of mild neuropathic bladder in all cases, with severe urinary tract damage in most of them. About two-thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation.

paragraphs.text: Derbent et al. (2009) reported what they described as the first published case of urofacial syndrome in Turkey. The patient was diagnosed at 16 years of age, after having been followed with the diagnosis of recurrent urinary tract infection and vesicoureteral reflux. The authors noted that the facial expression in this disorder is 'inverted,' such that patients appear to be crying when they smile, and that the urinary problems usually result in enuresis, urinary tract infection, and hydronephrosis, with some severely affected patients becoming hypertensive and progressing to end-stage renal disease.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1997) performed a genome screen using a combination of homozygosity mapping and DNA pooling in 20 selected patients with urofacial syndrome, 1 patient pool, and 3 control pools of unaffected relatives. After analysis of 36 randomly chosen markers, D10S677 was identified as linked to and associated with UFS, as suggested by a significant excess of homozygosity in patients compared with unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-6)) and by allele frequency differences between the patient pool and control pools. Fine mapping with 10 additional markers covering a 22-cM region by haplotype (linkage disequilibrium) analysis showed that all 31 patients were homozygous for 2 closely linked markers (D10S1726 and D10S198) located approximately 5 cM telomeric to D10S677, whereas only 12% of unaffected relatives were homozygous for both markers (P less than 10(-19)). Recombinational events at the flanking markers D10S1433 and D10S603 placed the UFS gene within a 1-cM interval on chromosome 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Derbent et al. (2009) advised that urofacial syndrome be considered in any patient who presents with dysfunctional voiding, particularly in countries with high rates of consanguineous marriage.

clinical_synopsis.feature: Abnormal caliber of prostatic and membranous urethra
End-stage renal disease in severely affected patients
Severe hypertrophy of bladder mucosa with sclerotic changes
Incomplete bladder voiding without anatomic outflow obstruction
Inverted facial expression when smiling or laughing (appear to cry when smiling)

allelic_variants.name: HPSE2, 10-KB DEL, EX8-9
hgvs: 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2

paragraphs.text: In an individual with urofacial syndrome, Daly et al. (2010) identified a homozygous 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene. The deletion was found within a 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24 defined by whole-genome SNP mapping.

checks.claim: Daly et al. (2010) identified a homozygous 10-kb deletion in the HPSE2 gene in an individual with urofacial syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24, within which a 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2 was identified
checks.explanation: The abstract does not use the word 'homozygous' for this patient. Homozygosity is inferred because the deletion lies within an autozygous region.

checks.claim: The 10-kb HPSE2 deletion identified by Daly et al. (2010) in an individual with urofacial syndrome encompasses exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2.
checks.evidence_quote: a 10 kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of HPSE2 was identified

checks.claim: The 16-Mb autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24 containing the HPSE2 deletion was defined by whole-genome SNP mapping.
checks.evidence_quote: Whole-genome SNP mapping in one affected individual defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24
